query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy protective coatings, a high density of semi‐coherent phase boundaries between the FCC matrix and the BCC phase acts as an intrinsic barrier that impedes stress‐assisted dislocation climb and glide. This interfacial barrier effect raises the effective activation energy for creep and increases the stress exponent during continuous loading, thereby imparting superior creep resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A dual-phase high-entropy alloy coating microstructure with roughly equiaxed FCC and BCC regions, featuring relatively flat (non‐serrated) and partially incoherent phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Modify the deposition or post-deposition heat treatment parameters to enhance the coherency and/or develop a serrated (undulated) morphology of the FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
generation.conditions: Continuous loading (constant stress) at intermediate to high temperatures (e.g., 500–600 °C) where creep is active, under comparable applied stresses that induce progressive plastic deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Semi‐coherent and/or serrated FCC/BCC phase boundaries that provide localized strain fields and act as physical obstacles to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced interfacial bonding and undulating (serrated) boundaries generate local interfacial stresses that impede dislocation climb and restrict cross-boundary slip. This barrier effect limits dynamic recrystallization and prevents the coarsening of deformation substructures, effectively increasing the creep activation energy and the stress exponent.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coating with less coherent or straight interfaces, the treated coating with enhanced semi‐coherent/serrated interfaces will exhibit a lower steady-state creep rate, increased stress exponent values, and a prolonged creep life. Microstructural analysis would show reduced dislocation density in the grain interiors and pronounced interfacial strain localization that retards dislocation pile-ups.
generation.baseline: Coatings processed under standard conditions exhibiting less controlled phase boundary features with relatively straight or incoherent interfaces.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under sustained stress in the intermediate-to-high temperature regime (approximately 500–600 °C) before potential phase instabilities or extensive recrystallization set in.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on evidence from the dynamic precipitation and recrystallization hindering dislocation motion in FCC HEAs (as noted in PMC7512559::web::022::5_conclusions and subsequent discussion) combined with the reported potent barrier effect of semi‐coherent phase boundaries in dual‐phase HEAs (PMC6175879::web::000::abstract). What is new here is extending the concept to FCC/BCC protective coatings and proposing that engineered boundary morphology (enhanced coherency and serration) can be used as a design lever to suppress progressive plastic deformation via kinetically impeding dislocation processes. The precise quantitative impact remains uncertain until experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy coatings. Process one set under standard deposition/annealing conditions (control) and the other set with a modified heat treatment designed to promote enhanced phase boundary coherency and serration. Subject both sets to identical creep testing under constant load at 500–600 °C. Post-deformation, perform microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM/SEM) to compare the dislocation structures and phase boundary characteristics.
measurements: Stress exponent (n) derived from creep rate vs. applied stress curves
Activation energy from temperature-dependent creep tests
Microstructural characterization of phase boundaries (coherency and serration level)
Dislocation density distribution near interfaces versus within grain interiors
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings with engineered (more coherent/serrated) phase boundaries do not exhibit a statistically significant lower steady-state creep rate, higher stress exponent, or show no discernible improvement in microstructural features related to dislocation hindrance compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis that enhanced interface morphology significantly contributes to improved creep resistance will be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSecond phase strengthening has been applied to high entropy alloys (HEAs) for optimizing mechanical properties. In this study, by conducting mechanical testing of a eutectic dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi HEA with homogenous distribution of body-centered cubic (BCC) and face-centered cubic (FCC) lamellar phases inside a transmission electron microscope, we found that although BCC was truly the hard phase, decreasing the proportion of BCC phase in fact increased the strength due to the existence of chemically disordered semi-coherent phase boundaries, which acted as potent impediments to dislocation motion resulting in dense dislocation storage in FCC phases. Moreover, the difficulty in dislocation glide caused massive cross-slip, and the interaction between primary slip arrays and cross-slip systems during deformation increased the rate of dislocation accumulation by forming dislocation substructures, thus making the FCC phases exceptionally strong. Our findings not only revealed the underlying strengthening mechanism of eutectic dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi HEAs, but also shed light on new ways in further optimizing the mechanical properties of HEAs.

The intermediate-temperature creep behavior and microstructural evolution of CoCrFeNiMn HEA have been studied. Optical micrographs and TEM images of the dislocation substructure after creep deformation revealed the effects of dynamic recrystallization and dynamic precipitation on the deformation mechanisms. The following conclusions can be drawn:An obvious transition in stress exponent and average activation energy was observed: At low stresses, the values were approximately 5 to 6 and 268 kJ/mol, whereas at high-stress regions, the corresponding values were 8.9–14 and 380 kJ/mol. Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion is suggested as a possible rate-dominating mechanism at low stresses.At high stresses, obvious dynamic recrystallization occurred, leading to the refinement of average grain size. Simultaneously, nano-sized M23C6 carbides and the Cr-rich tetragonal σ phase were dynamically precipitated. High density of tangled and curved dislocation substructures was observed.
